data.title: Middle East Eye: Morning update
data.author: Hilal Saki
data.summary:
Morning update
Good Morning Middle East Eye readers,
If you are just joining us, here are key developments from across the region and beyond:
*Two Houthi ballistic missiles and three drones, aimed at Saudi Arabia's Eastern Region and Riyadh, were intercepted and destroyed, according to the Saudi-led coalition.
*Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said their forces carried out a drone attack on a US radar system at a base in Bahrain.
*Bahraini air defence systems intercepted and neutralised several Iran aerial attacks on Sunday, Bahrain Defence Force said in a statement, accusing Iran of continuing its "systematic hostile approach through its malicious attacks" on the kingdom.
*Hamas' armed wing said on Sunday that a senior commander, Samir Abu Younis, 53, who commanded its Rafah brigade, was killed in an Israeli airstrike.
*Two oil tankers struck naval mines as they tried to cross the Strait of Hormuz “secretly”, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Navy says.
*Israeli settlers stormed the al-Harayeq area of the town of Beita, south of Nablus in the occupied West Bank, and attacked the home of Palestinian citizen Mutie Salim Qutish.
*Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi dismissed nine officials on Saturday, following an investigation into allegations of oil smuggling in the Jurf al-Sakher area, a stronghold of the Iran-backed Kataeb Hezbollah group.
*American intelligence believes that Iran has some 1,500-2,500 missiles, and the apparent size of the arsenal has impacted Trump administration's decision on whether to resume strikes on the Islamic Republic, The Wall Street Journal reported.
*A car bomb killed two people, including a child, and wounded another, in a suburb of Damascus on Saturday, Syrian Arab News Agency (Sana) said.
*President Donald Trump has told senior advisers in recent days that he may hold off on attacking Iran if the US faces no new provocations from Tehran or the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen, Reuters reported.

data.title: Middle East Eye: ‘Looking away was never a choice for me’: How Hollywood’s love affair with Israel turned sour
data.author: Fleur Hargreaves
data.summary:
‘Looking away was never a choice for me’: How Hollywood’s love affair with Israel turned sour
Submitted by
Fleur Hargreaves
on
Mon, 11/02/2026 - 10:59
A growing number of actors and film workers have been challenging their industry’s ‘deep complicity’ with Israel to end the toxic relationship
US actress Hannah Einbinder wears an 'Artists4Ceasefire' pin as she attends the 83rd annual Golden Globe Awards at the Beverly Hilton hotel in Beverly Hills, California, on 11 January 2026 (Frederic J Brown/AFP)
Off
Once Israel could rely on Hollywood to have its reputation laundered, performing the role of a benign ally which shared the values and interests of the West.
However, a growing number of actors and prominent figures in film and TV are confronting the industry’s ongoing complicity with Israel's occupation and its actions in Gaza, which a consensus of experts and human rights groups have called a genocide.
More and more artists are using their platforms to speak about the plight of the Palestinians and have contributed to Israel’s cratering approval among western audiences.
In 2025, US-based organisation Film Workers for Palestine (FWP), established by a group of filmmakers the previous year, released a pledge to end complicity with the genocide in Gaza.
It garnered the signatures of more than 5,500 people in the industry, including A-list actors like Josh O’Connor, Olivia Colman, Andrew Garfield, Emma Stone and many more.
Inspired by Filmmakers United Against Apartheid, a group of artists who refused to screen their work in apartheid South Africa, signatories pledged not to screen films, appear at or work alongside Israeli film institutions implicated in genocide and apartheid.
“People were ready to publicly put their name to a commitment of refusal... to not be complicit in Israel’s genocide,” an FWP spokesperson told Middle East Eye, adding that there is “power in numbers”.

France accused Shahid Kaveh, an offensive cyber unit within the IRGC’s Electronic Warfare and Cyber Defence Organisation, of carrying out the cyber attacks.
The attacks targeted refrigeration control systems at over 700 retail outlets on the night of 11-12 October, causing fires, serious damage and losses of food worth tens of millions of euros, the French foreign ministry said.
Paris said it would summon Iran's ambassador and propose new sanctions against individuals and entities within the European Union.

While the US does not release official demographic breakdowns of voting patterns, an estimated 680,000 people of Pakistani origin lived in the country in 2023, according to the Pew Research Center.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Israel's data shows it allowed half of the promised aid trucks into Gaza
data.author: Elis Gjevori
data.summary:
Israel's data shows it allowed half of the promised aid trucks into Gaza
Israel has failed to meet its commitments under the Gaza ceasefire deal, allowing in only around half the agreed volume of humanitarian and commercial goods each month since March, Israeli military data shows.
Data obtained by Haaretz newspaper showed a growing shortfall in food deliveries to Gaza, alongside severe shortages of medical supplies, tents and materials to repair damaged infrastructure. Torrential rains have flooded displacement camps, leaving hundreds of thousands of Palestinians in increasingly dire conditions.
Under the ceasefire deal, Israel pledged to allow 4,200 vehicles carrying humanitarian and commercial goods into Gaza each week, equivalent to roughly 18,200 a month.
Deliveries were to include food, fuel, medical supplies and equipment, shelter materials and equipment to repair essential infrastructure.
Data supplied by the Coordinator of Government Activities in the Territories (Cogat) to the US-led International Gaza Support Center (IGSC) show that Israel allowed about 4,700 trucks into Gaza in March, rising to 5,300 in April and more than 9,600 in May.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Exclusive: Toyota reviewing use of forklifts by Israeli military after MEE investigation
data.author: Elis Gjevori
data.summary:
Exclusive: Toyota reviewing use of forklifts by Israeli military after MEE investigation
Toyota has said it is investigating the use of its forklifts by the Israeli military after Middle East Eye found photos and videos of the vehicles at weapons and munitions storage sites, serving supply lines for frontline units, and being used by the army’s Logistics Corps.
It comes after MEE uncovered details of a previously unreported 158m-shekel ($49.8m) contract between Toyota and Israel’s Ministry of Defense for the supply of forklifts that was signed in 2024 – the first full year of the Gaza war.
Toyota says that its vehicles are not intended for military use.
When asked about the contract, the company told MEE it had commitments in place with both the defence ministry and its official reseller in Israel to ensure that its technology and products were “for civil use only”.
But when MEE then shared footage posted on official Israeli military social media channels, which showed Toyota forklifts being used at locations including a missiles and ammunition depot in northern Israel, a Logistics Corps training base, and inside a munitions factory, it said it was investigating the images to determine whether those agreements had been breached.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Yemen hospital faces shutdown risk due to sege on Taiz
data.author: Mera Aladam
data.summary:
Yemen hospital faces shutdown risk due to sege on Taiz
A hospital in the Yemeni city of Taiz has sounded the alarm over medicine and fuel shortages, warning that it is facing the risk of a shutdown if access to aid and supplies is not restored.
"For two months we have been calling and appealing to the international community, the humanitarian organisations: save Taiz, save health in Taiz, save the Yemeni-Swedish hospital. There is no fuel. We are at our last breath," said the hospital director Sami Al-Sharabi.
The Houthis have besieged Taiz for more than a month as they try to break into territory held by the Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces.
Since fighting reignited in the summer, nearly 330,000 people have been displaced.
"Save Taiz, save health in Taiz, save the Yemeni-Swedish hospital. There is no fuel. We are at our last breath."
